item.title: Gold hits 1-year low near $3,830, on course for worst year since 2015 as yields bite
item.description:
Gold is being driven by rates and the dollar, not by geopolitics. Escalation in the Middle East works against it: higher oil feeds inflation, which feeds Fed hike expectations. That makes the December FOMC decision and US inflation data the key catalysts, and any repricing toward a 50 basis point hike would add pressure. The $3,800 area is the nearest support. A clean break would expose the metal to further ETF liquidation. For FX, gold’s slide adds to the headwinds facing the Australian dollar, which is already near its weakest levels since January.

---

Gold has given up more than 30% from January’s record as rising yields and a strong dollar outweigh its inflation-hedge appeal. Analysts warn that the next leg lower could come from ETF holders heading for the exit.

Summary:

  • Gold fell to a one-year low near $3,830 an ounce, more than 30% below January’s record of around $5,595.
  • The metal is on course for its worst year since 2015.
  • Treasury yields above 5%, a dollar near its highest since April 2025 and expectations of a December Fed hike are weighing on prices.
  • Analysts warn that ETF investors could start selling after a drop of almost 7% in a matter of days.
  • Goldman Sachs now sees gold at $4,150 by end-2026 and $4,650 by end-2027. (Goldman’s second gold forecast downgrade in a month turns its bear case into the base case)
  • Central bank buying and ETF inflows offer longer-term support. Poland has reached its reserve target, though, and demand for bars and coins has fallen.

Gold fell to a one-year low on Monday, according to a Reuters analysis. High Treasury yields, a firm US dollar and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy weighed on the metal, leaving bullion on course for its worst year since 2015.

Prices touched around $3,830 an ounce, the lowest since early October 2025 and more than 30% below January’s record of about $5,595. Spot gold was trading near $3,860 early in the Asian session on Tuesday, holding just above the closely watched $3,800 area.

The pressure is coming from rates. Markets expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points in December, with a small chance of a larger move, and the 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%. The dollar is hovering near its highest since April 2025, which makes bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies. The US-Israeli war on Iran has pushed up oil prices and inflation. Gold is often seen as a hedge against inflation, but it tends to lose its appeal when rates are rising.

Analysts have turned more bearish as the $4,000 level gave way. Some noted that gold lost almost 7%, or around $290, in a matter of days last week. That was a faster drop than the move in rate expectations alone would suggest, and they warned that investors in exchange-traded funds could start selling into the weakness, deepening the decline. Others pointed to stress in equity markets, with Nvidia’s market value down around $1.9 trillion since early October. They said gold is often sold to raise cash in the short term.

Goldman Sachs has cut its gold forecasts twice this month and now sees the metal at $4,150 by the end of 2026 and $4,650 by the end of 2027.

The longer-term demand picture is more mixed. Physically backed gold ETFs took in 211 metric tons in the third quarter, and central banks bought 675 tons in the first nine months of the year. However, Poland, the most active official buyer, has reached its 700-ton reserve target, and demand for bars and coins has fallen sharply. China remains a steady buyer.

Some analysts argue that central bank buying and resilient ETF holdings may help limit the correction. They also say that support is unlikely to stop further short-term weakness if yields and the dollar keep rising. The $3,800 area is the next level to watch.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA minutes: 6 members saw rates “not clearly sufficient”, 3 warned of sharper downturn
item.description:
On balance the minutes lean hawkish, unsurpisngly. The majority’s view that 4.85% is “not clearly sufficient” sits awkwardly with market pricing that had all but ruled out further hikes, and it backs up Bullock’s comment this morning about upside risks. The minority’s warning of a sharper downturn sets a high bar for a December move, though. This week’s wage and jobs data, and the October CPI jump the staff flagged in advance, matter more than usual. For the Australian dollar, near 0.6730, the minutes are mildly supportive but unlikely to change the trend while policy diverges from the Fed. The minutes treat oil as the swing factor: if prices hold rather than ease by around US$30 a barrel as assumed, the inflation case for another hike strengthens.

---

Earlier

  • RBA’s Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes

---

The RBA majority hiked because 4.85% might not be enough, and the minority held back because the economy might already be cracking. That leaves the next move hostage to this week’s jobs data and the oil price.

Summary:

  • Six of nine RBA board members backed November’s hike to 4.85%, judging the cash rate “not clearly sufficient” to address upside inflation risks.
  • The majority cited strong market services inflation, high unit labour costs, broad cost pressures and a likely rise in the neutral rate.
  • Three members preferred to hold, warning the economy might be near a materially sharper downturn as unemployment rose half a point in six months.
  • Inflation forecasts assume oil falls by around US$30 a barrel over two years, which leaves significant upside risk if prices stay high.
  • Staff expect headline inflation to jump in October as last year’s energy subsidies drop out.
  • The board gave no explicit forward guidance beyond staying attentive to the data.

Most Reserve Bank of Australia board members judged that the cash rate was “not clearly sufficient” to bring inflation under control when they voted to raise it to 4.85% this month, according to minutes of the November meeting released on Tuesday. A three-member minority warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn.

The minutes lay bare a board divided over the balance of risks. The six members who backed the 25 basis point increase, the fifth hike of the year, said forward-looking inflation pressures had risen and the risks to the outlook remained to the upside. They judged that the danger of leaving policy insufficiently restrictive, and allowing inflation expectations to drift higher, outweighed the risk of tightening too much.

The majority pointed to three signs that domestic capacity pressures were playing a bigger role than previously thought: strong inflation in market services, persistent growth in unit labour costs, and broad-based cost pressures reported by business contacts. Staff have revised up their estimate of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, which implies the labour market was tighter in 2026 than they had assessed. Members also noted that the neutral interest rate had likely risen, which makes any given cash rate less restrictive than before.

The three dissenters preferred to hold at 4.60%. They argued it was prudent to wait and assess the 100 basis points of tightening already delivered this year. They placed more weight on downside risks to growth, citing a half-percentage-point rise in unemployment over six months, the housing downturn and fragile sentiment toward investment in data centres.

The Middle East conflict featured heavily. Members noted that crude and refined fuel prices had risen 20% to 25% since August. The forecasts assume oil prices fall by around US$30 a barrel over two years, an assumption that requires some resolution of the conflict and leaves significant upside risk if prices stay high. Staff expect headline inflation to jump in October as last year’s energy subsidies drop out.

The board offered no explicit guidance, saying only that it will remain attentive to the data and do what is necessary to return inflation to target. Earlier on Tuesday, Governor Michele Bullock said inflation risks are still skewed to the upside. Wage data on Wednesday and October jobs figures on Thursday are the next tests.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6715 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US warns Americans in Europe of holiday terror risk as bomb hoaxes disrupt flights
item.description:
The alert is precautionary, and alerts like this rarely move markets on their own. The bigger point for markets is travel reliability heading into the busiest stretch of the year. US carriers are still clearing backlogs from last week’s FAA ground stop, and Monday’s United outage shows how little slack there is in airline systems. Any further disruption in Europe or the US during the Thanksgiving peak would bring airline and travel stocks into focus. The banking outages were resolved and described as technical. They’re more a reminder of operational risk than a credit or stability concern.

---

Also:

  • Iran drawing up dirty bomb options for Washington, 7 US officials say, not seen imminent

---

Washington is warning Americans to watch their step in Europe this holiday season. Back home, a week of grounded flights and frozen bank apps has shown that the systems people rely on can fail without any attacker involved.

Summary:

  • The US Embassy in Bulgaria issued a Europe-wide security alert urging Americans to stay vigilant during the holiday season.
  • It warns that terrorists, including lone actors, could target markets, transport hubs, malls and places of worship with little warning.
  • Strikes and demonstrations have become more frequent, and hoax bomb threats disrupted flights in numerous European countries in November.
  • Americans are advised to monitor local news, check with airlines, avoid demonstrations and enroll in the State Department’s STEP alert program.
  • In the US, an FAA ground stop, a United Airlines outage and online banking problems at major lenders caused disruption in recent days.
  • No agency or company has linked the US incidents to a cyberattack or a foreign actor.

The US Embassy in Bulgaria has issued a Europe-wide security alert urging American citizens to stay vigilant over the holiday season. It warns that terrorists, including lone actors, may strike with little or no warning, and that disruptions to travel and daily life remain possible across the continent.

The alert, dated November 16, says large gatherings and public events could be a target for terrorist groups and criminals. It singles out tourist locations such as markets, transport hubs, shopping malls and places of worship, and urges extra caution at holiday festivals and other crowded events.

On disruption, the embassy notes that strikes and demonstrations have become more frequent in recent months. It also says hoax bomb threats targeted civil aviation in numerous European countries in November, disrupting flights. Americans are advised to:

  • monitor local news and check with their airline for disruptions
  • avoid demonstrations and areas with heavy police activity
  • keep a low profile
  • enroll in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program for security updates

The warning comes after a run of disruption on the US side of the Atlantic. A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop on Friday halted departures for several hours and led to around 10,000 cancellations. The government blamed a communications failure during equipment work. On Monday, United Airlines suffered a short-lived systemwide technology outage. The same day, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other major lenders reported problems accessing online banking.

No agency or company has tied any of those US incidents to a cyberattack or a foreign actor. The FAA said its investigation found no sign of an attack, and United and Chase both said their problems were technical rather than cyber-related. Given Trump's wars I'd be sceptical of these glib explanantions. Regardless, the cluster has highlighted how exposed travel and payments are to technical failures at a busy time of year.

The timing matters for travellers. US airlines expect close to 29 million passengers over the Thanksgiving period from November 20 to 30. Europe’s holiday season brings the large markets and crowds the embassy alert focuses on. For now the advice is precautionary, and the alert does not cite a specific threat. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China resumes crude stockpiling, leaving room for fuel exports at 3 times prewar margins
item.description:
For crude, China’s return to stockpiling adds a source of demand alongside refinery consumption. That supports import levels even while runs are soft, and helps cushion prices against weaker demand elsewhere. The bigger lever is in products. With refineries running below 80% and diesel margins near triple their prewar level, more export quotas from Beijing could send significant volumes of fuel into Asian markets and narrow those margins. For now the signal points the other way: diesel exports are falling and November tracking is weaker. The tightness in middle distillates looks set to persist unless policy changes.

---

China has come through the Hormuz shock with its oil reserves intact and is rebuilding again. It also has plenty of idle refining capacity, so whether diesel margins stay this high depends largely on Beijing’s export quotas.

Summary:

  • China added close to 490,000 bpd of crude to its stockpiles in October, reversing a draw of around 530,000 bpd in September.
  • Crude imports rose to about 9.9 million bpd, the highest since March, while refinery runs slipped to around 13.7 million bpd.
  • Over the first 10 months of 2026, China has still added about 270,000 bpd to its inventories despite the disruption from the Iran war.
  • Fuel exports fell to about 5.2 million tons in October, and diesel exports dropped to around 310,000 bpd from a near three-year high in September.
  • Refineries are running at less than 80% of capacity, so there’s scope to increase exports.
  • The Singapore gasoil margin is near $59 a barrel, almost three times its prewar level.

China resumed stockpiling crude oil in October for the first time since July, as imports recovered and refinery processing stayed soft, according to a very good piece by Reuters columnist Clyde Russell. That gives Beijing room to raise fuel exports if it chooses to.

Russell calculates from official data that refiners processed close to 490,000 barrels per day less in October than the crude available to them from imports and domestic production. China doesn’t disclose flows into or out of its strategic and commercial reserves, but the gap between available supply and refinery runs gives an estimate. October’s surplus reversed a draw of around 530,000 bpd in September.

Crude imports rose to about 9.9 million bpd, up more than 9% from September and the highest since March. Domestic output was around 4.3 million bpd. Refinery throughput slipped about 2% to roughly 13.7 million bpd.

Since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, China has drawn on its inventories in May, June, August and September, with only a small build in July. Over the first 10 months of the year, however, it has still added around 270,000 bpd to stockpiles, Russell notes. Strong builds before the war and October’s rebound have offset the drawdowns. In other words, China has come through the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the early months of the conflict without running down its reserves.

Lower refinery runs have also cut fuel exports, which fell to about 5.2 million metric tons in October from around 7.2 million in September. Exports depend on government quotas, not market forces. Refiners were told to curb shipments early in the conflict to protect domestic supply, before the restrictions were eased so they could capture strong margins. Diesel exports reached about 500,000 bpd in September, the most in nearly three years. They fell to around 310,000 bpd in October, and early November tracking points lower again.

With China’s refining system running at less than 80% of capacity, there is ample room to raise output. The incentive is clear: the Singapore gasoil margin, the benchmark for diesel, ended Monday at around $59 a barrel. That is nearly three times the roughly $21 it stood at the day before the war began. Whether Beijing issues more export quotas will decide if that spare capacity reaches global fuel markets. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes
item.description:
Bullock’s comment pushes back modestly against market pricing that has all but ruled out a December hike. It could offer the Australian dollar some support after it fell this week to its lowest level since late January. One line on a panel is unlikely to shift pricing on its own, so the minutes are the bigger test. Any sign that the majority on the board saw a real chance of further tightening would firm up the hawkish reading of Bullock’s remarks. If the minutes play up how close the vote was, front-end rates may decide the governor’s comment is a hedge, not a signal.

-

Minutes preview here:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock

-

Bullock says inflation risks are still tilted higher. That reminds markets that a split board doesn’t mean the RBA is done, just as the minutes are due to show how close the debate was.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock says inflation risks remain skewed to the upside.
  • She made the remarks at a panel in Sydney, shortly before the release of the November meeting minutes.
  • The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth hike this year and the highest level since 2008, in a 6-3 vote.
  • Markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December rate rise.
  • The minutes are expected to show how the board weighed inflation risks against a slowing economy.
  • Wage data on Wednesday and October jobs figures on Thursday round out the week.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said on Tuesday that the risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, Reuters reported. Her remarks come shortly before the release of minutes from the central bank’s November meeting.

Speaking on a panel at the ASIC Annual Forum in Sydney, Bullock said the board’s current view is that inflation risks are still skewed higher. The comment was brief, but its timing matters. Since the November decision, markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December rate rise. Her words suggest the board is not yet ready to declare its tightening campaign over.

The RBA lifted its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth increase this year and the highest level since 2008. The vote was unusually split: six board members backed the hike and three preferred to hold at 4.60%. That division led many analysts to conclude the bank is close to the end of its cycle.

The minutes, due at 11.30am Sydney time (0030 GMT, 7.30pm ET on Monday), should shed more light on that debate. Analysts will look at how the board weighed inflation risks against a slowing economy, whether the three dissenters judged policy already restrictive enough, and how high the bar now is for a further move. The RBA’s own assessment puts the cash rate slightly above the top of its range of neutral rate estimates. Its forecasts have inflation staying above 3% until late 2027.

Bullock’s warning about upside risks sits alongside that restrictive stance. The board may judge that rates are high enough for now, while still wanting to keep the option of another hike open if inflation does not ease as expected.

The domestic calendar is busy for the rest of the week. Third-quarter wage price data is due on Wednesday and October employment figures on Thursday, when unemployment is expected to hold at 4.7%. Firm readings on either would test the market’s conviction that the RBA has finished hiking. 

Bullock heading out of the office to buy half a cup of coffee.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran drawing up dirty bomb options for Washington, 7 US officials say, not seen imminent
item.description:
For oil, the report adds to the escalation risks around a conflict that is already disrupting Hormuz shipping. The planning is described as optional rather than imminent, though, so it adds to tail risk more than to near-term supply pressure. The more market-relevant point is the regional source’s warning that hardliners who benefit from the war could try to wreck talks over the coming weeks. That keeps the outlook for a deal to reopen the strait fragile. A US homeland incident is a low-probability event with severe consequences. It would probably hit risk assets broadly, and more as a shock to risk appetite than as a direct supply story for crude.

---

US officials say Iran has drawn up specific options for a dirty bomb or chemical attack on Washington. It is not seen as imminent, but it shows how far Tehran’s incentive to escalate has grown under US pressure.

Summary:

  • New US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could target senior administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon.
  • Officials see the planning as Iran building options, not as a sign of an imminent attack, although the intelligence reportedly includes specific locations and targets.
  • The White House says there are no credible threats to the homeland. Iran rejected the chemical weapons allegations as fabricated.
  • Threats from Iran led the Secret Service to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing last week.
  • Separate intelligence suggests Iran could use chemical weapons against US troops in the Middle East.
  • Talks to end the US blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled, and the next few weeks are seen as critical.

New US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, CNN reported, citing seven US officials. Sources familiar with the intelligence described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not a sign that an attack is imminent.

Even so, two of the sources said the plotting picked up by US agencies has been very specific, including locations and targets. Officials have held several meetings over the past week on contingency plans to counter it. They remain divided over whether Iran has the capability or the people in place to carry out such a plot, or the intent to try.

The White House said the US is monitoring all potential threats but that there are currently no credible threats to the homeland. Iran’s mission to the United Nations rejected what it called false and fabricated allegations, saying Tehran considers the use of chemical weapons illegitimate under any circumstances. It did not directly address the dirty bomb intelligence.

US officials see the planning as a sign that Iran is more willing to escalate as it comes under intense pressure from US strikes and an economic blockade. One source put it this way: Iran’s capability has not changed, but its incentive has. According to the report, threats from Iran also led the Secret Service to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing last week.

A dirty bomb wraps radioactive material around a conventional explosive and is very different from a nuclear weapon. Experts say casualties would most likely come from the blast itself, though contamination could make areas unusable. Officials are separately monitoring intelligence that Iran could use chemical weapons against US troops in the Middle East. Several said troops lack adequate protective equipment or training.

The threats come as talks to end the US blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. A regional source said the next several weeks will be critical for any agreement, and warned that hardliners who have benefited from the war could try to play spoiler. One US official said Iran understands the retaliation it would face if it used such weapons. That calculation could shift, however, if Tehran comes to see the regime’s survival as at stake.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock keeps 5-year US equity overweight on AI conviction despite tactical caution
item.description:
BlackRock’s split view separates long-term allocation from short-term positioning. That gives investors a framework for holding US equities through AI-driven volatility, not chasing or dumping them. Its higher interest rate assumptions and its shift to neutral on developed-market government bonds suggest higher yields are starting to attract long-term buyers. The stronger overweight in inflation-linked bonds points to lasting inflation risk from supply constraints, including energy. Upcoming inflation data from Japan and the euro zone will show whether those energy costs are spreading into broader prices.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply

--- BlackRock is staying cautious on US stocks in the short term, but it is backing them for five years and more. Its bet is that AI adoption, not today’s winners or today’s earnings, will drive returns.

Summary:

  • BlackRock’s long-term conviction in AI underpins its strategic overweight in US equities over five years or longer, despite a tactical downgrade last month.
  • The view rests on AI’s improving capabilities and wider adoption, not on current earnings or market leaders.
  • Health care, IT, tech and financials are seen as having the strongest long-term earnings prospects.
  • Risks include overcapacity, squeezed supplier profits and adoption bottlenecks. The Shiller CAPE is around 41x, near dot-com highs, while the forward P/E of around 19x relies on strong earnings growth.
  • Competition for capital has led BlackRock to raise its rate expectations, and it sees policy rates staying higher for longer.
  • It has moved to neutral on developed-market government bonds and strengthened its overweight in inflation-linked bonds.

BlackRock says its long-term conviction in the AI transformation continues to underpin its strategic overweight in US equities, even though near-term risks justify a more cautious tactical stance. The world’s largest asset manager downgraded US stocks on a tactical basis last month. Its latest capital market assumptions, however, reinforce the overweight over a horizon of five years or longer.

The distinction matters. BlackRock says its longer-term view rests on AI’s improving capabilities and wider adoption over time, not on today’s earnings growth or on current market leaders staying on top. Its starting-point scenario explicitly assumes valuations will decline and does not rely on a permanent growth breakout. Even so, broader AI adoption could lift productivity, profit margins and earnings. It sees health care, IT, tech and financials as offering the strongest longer-term earnings prospects.

The near-term caution reflects genuine uncertainty over how the AI buildout develops relative to demand. Falling computing costs could squeeze suppliers’ profits, while bottlenecks could slow adoption. Overcapacity is a risk, and the companies building AI infrastructure could see earnings slow before the businesses using it see meaningful gains. On valuations, the measure matters. The S&P 500’s Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which uses 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings, stands at around 41 times. That is not far below its dot-com era peak in the mid-40s. The 12-month forward multiple, at around 19 times, looks far less stretched, but only because investors expect strong earnings growth.

Funding the buildout is another theme. Companies financing AI investment are competing with heavily borrowing governments for the same pool of savings, which has prompted BlackRock to raise its interest rate expectations. It expects central bank policy rates to stay higher for longer, reflecting a higher neutral rate. It argues, though, that stronger growth and earnings can coexist with higher borrowing costs.

That repricing has made bonds more attractive. For the first time since 2020, BlackRock is taking a more constructive view on duration. It has moved to neutral on developed-market government bonds and strengthened its overweight in inflation-linked bonds. It cautions, however, that government bonds are no longer the reliable diversifiers they once were, because persistent inflation limits how far central banks can cut.

In the near term, BlackRock is watching fresh inflation data from Japan and the euro zone for signs of how higher energy costs are feeding into price pressures.

The S&P 500’s Shiller CAPE is near dot-com era highs, but the forward P/E looks far less stretched because it relies on expected earnings growth. Source: BlackRock Investment Institute, LSEG Datastream, November 2026.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran says 4th tanker hit in 24 hours as UKMTO reports Hormuz attack near Oman
item.description:
For oil, an attack in the narrowest part of the Strait of Hormuz hits the main export route for Gulf crude directly. That supports the risk premium even before any supply loss is confirmed. Crude has recently held back from reacting to unverified Iranian claims, so independent confirmation of multiple strikes is the trigger to watch for a sharper move. Higher war-risk insurance premiums and owners rerouting or delaying transits would tighten effective supply even if no cargo is lost. The US force-protection build-up suggests Washington is not expecting a quick de-escalation.

---

An attack in the narrowest part of Hormuz has left a tanker disabled and on fire. Iran says it has now hit four in a day, and the US is pouring concrete for a long stay.

Summary:

  • A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 1900 GMT on Monday.
  • The attack caused an engine room fire. The crew are reported safe, and damage and environmental impact are not yet known.
  • Iran’s navy says it has hit four oil tankers in the past 24 hours. The link to this incident is not confirmed.
  • Tehran claimed over the weekend that a supertanker sank after hitting a mine, which remains unverified.
  • The US Army is seeking 17 concrete bunkers for bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon within 45 days, citing risks to troops from Iranian fire.
  • A third US carrier strike group has arrived in the region.

A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack on Monday that left it with an engine room fire, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency. Iran’s navy claimed it had now hit four oil tankers in the past 24 hours.

UKMTO said it received a third-party report of the incident about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, on Oman’s Musandam peninsula, at 1900 GMT (2 pm ET). The crew were reported safe, but the extent of the damage and any environmental impact were not yet known. The agency advised vessels to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity while authorities investigate.

The Iranian navy’s announcement of a fourth tanker strike appears to relate to the same incident. That link has not been independently confirmed, and UKMTO did not identify the vessel or say who carried out the attack. Over the weekend, Tehran also claimed that a supertanker had sunk after hitting a mine, a claim that has yet to be verified.

Khasab sits on the southern side of the strait’s narrowest stretch, where the inbound and outbound shipping lanes run close to the Omani coast. An attack there goes to the heart of the main export route for Gulf crude.

The escalation at sea comes as Washington prepares for a longer confrontation. The US Army is seeking to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers at bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon within 45 days. The bunkers will replace converted shipping containers that the Army says leave soldiers at risk from Iranian missile and drone fire. A third US aircraft carrier strike group has also reportedly arrived in the region, joining two already deployed.

Taken together, the tanker strikes and the US build-up in protection for its forces point to a conflict that both sides are preparing to sustain rather than wind down. For shipping, the immediate questions are whether the latest vessel can be identified and whether independent reports bear out Iran’s count of four strikes. Also watch how insurers and owners respond to a fresh attack so close to Oman’s coast. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Intel slides 7% as investors sue over PC slump disclosures, extends losses after hours
item.description:
A lawsuit rarely changes a company’s fundamentals, but this one keeps attention on Intel’s weakest point, the PC business, at a time when the stock has already lost about half its value in six months. The supply argument cuts both ways. Shortages of substrates and memory limit how fast Intel can capture data center demand, and they also weigh on PC makers. That ties into the industry-wide memory squeeze flagged by Goldman Sachs. Nvidia’s results are the next big test of chip sentiment. Any sign that supply constraints are loosening across the sector would matter more to Intel’s shares than the legal case.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply

---

Investors are suing Intel. They allege its upbeat AI talk masked a worsening PC slump and supply shortages, and the lawsuit reopens the wound from October’s record one-day plunge.

Summary:

  • Intel shares closed about 7% lower on Monday near $55.50 and fell around 3% further after hours.
  • A proposed class action filed on Friday alleges Intel misled investors about the hit from slowing PC sales and excess inventory.
  • The complaint also alleges Intel concealed that supply limits prevented it from meeting data center demand.
  • The suit covers investors who bought shares between July 23 and October 29.
  • October’s results sparked a one-day fall of nearly 29%, wiping out around $140 billion of market value.
  • The stock is down nearly 50% over six months after a strong rally earlier in the year.

Intel shares fell about 7% on Monday after investors filed a proposed class action accusing the chipmaker of misleading the market about how a slowdown in PC sales was hurting its business. The stock closed near $55.50 and slipped a further 3% or so in after-hours trade to around $53.70. 

The lawsuit was filed on Friday in federal court in San Jose, California. It is led by a Michigan public pension fund, the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, and was brought by the law firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd. It seeks to represent investors who bought Intel shares between July 23 and October 29 this year.

The complaint alleges that Intel played down the damage from weakening PC demand and a build-up of excess inventory. It also alleges that Intel concealed that supply limits were preventing it from meeting demand from data centers. According to the filing, gains from data center construction and the wider AI boom were more than offset by the PC slowdown.

The plaintiffs point to earlier upbeat comments from management. In January, chief executive Lip-Bu Tan said Intel was positioned to capture “unprecedented demand” from AI infrastructure projects. In July, chief financial officer David Zinsner said a softer PC market would let the company shift production toward data center processors. On the October earnings call, however, Zinsner said Intel faced severe supply constraints. These included a shortage of substrates, a key material used in chip packaging, which undercut the earlier argument.

The October results triggered a drop of nearly 29% the following day. That wiped around $140 billion off Intel’s market value, its steepest one-day fall in more than half a century. The shares have now lost close to half their value over the past six months, after a strong rally earlier in the year.

Securities class actions of this kind usually take months or years to resolve. So the immediate question for the market is less about legal liability. It is more about whether Intel can show that its supply constraints are easing and that data center demand can make up for weakness in PCs.

Not smiling ATM

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply
item.description:
If Goldman is right that the market is already pricing in an earnings slowdown that hasn’t arrived, beaten-down chip names could recover quickly on any upbeat earnings or guidance. Nvidia’s results are an obvious near-term test. The memory squeeze matters well beyond the US. It feeds directly into Asian chip heavyweights such as Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC, and so into the Kospi and Taiwan’s benchmark. The stress on selectivity points to dispersion rather than a sector-wide rebound. Memory, equipment and supply-chain names look better placed than the most crowded GPU trades.

---

Chip stocks are priced as if an earnings downturn is coming, but Goldman sees demand running ahead of supply and multi-year visibility. It argues the sell-off has created buying opportunities for investors who choose carefully.

Summary:

  • Semiconductor stocks have sold off sharply in recent weeks even as fundamentals have strengthened.
  • Demand is running ahead of supply in memory, server CPUs and chipmaking equipment. Memory makers are signing multi-year supply deals, and equipment suppliers are planning for higher spending into 2027 and 2028.
  • Demand is broadening beyond GPUs into high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, networking and power. Tight memory supply is now hitting PCs and consumer devices too.
  • Nvidia’s leadership transition is seen as more likely to shift market share gradually than to disrupt the AI investment cycle.
  • The sector trades at about 13x forward earnings. That is roughly a third below its three-year average of 19x, close to its three-year low and below the S&P 500 multiple.
  • The correction offers more attractive entry points, but competitive, geopolitical and supply-chain risks make selectivity important.

Goldman Sachs says the recent sell-off in semiconductor stocks has left the sector’s valuations badly out of step with its improving fundamentals. It argues the correction is creating more attractive entry points for investors who are prepared to be selective.

Chip shares have fallen sharply in recent weeks, yet the bank notes that the latest earnings season showed demand running ahead of supply in several parts of the industry. Memory, server processors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment stand out. Companies are also talking about visibility well beyond the next few quarters. Memory makers are locking in multi-year supply agreements, and equipment suppliers are planning for higher wafer fabrication spending into 2027 and 2028.

The opportunity is also widening, according to Goldman. Demand is spreading beyond graphics processors into CPUs, high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, networking and power. Tight memory supply is becoming a constraint across the whole industry, affecting PCs and other consumer devices as well as AI infrastructure.

On Nvidia, Goldman sees the company’s leadership transition as more likely to shift market share within the sector than to derail the broader AI investment cycle. Because supply is constrained and chip design cycles are long, any such shifts should be gradual. They could broaden the range of winners across GPUs, custom silicon and the supporting supply chain.

Valuations, meanwhile, have moved the other way. The semiconductor group now trades at roughly 13 times forward earnings. That is about a third below its three-year average of 19 times and close to its three-year low of around 12.7 times. The group also trades below the S&P 500 multiple, even though it has historically traded at a premium to the broader market.

Goldman stresses that the discount does not remove the risks. Competitive dynamics remain fluid, and geopolitical and supply-chain factors could add uncertainty across the sector. Instead, the bank argues, the market appears to be pricing in a meaningful drop in future earnings that has yet to show up in demand or earnings expectations. The practical takeaway is that the case for chips now depends less on the sector as a whole and more on picking the companies best placed for the next phase of AI spending.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand food prices fall 0.4% in October as RBNZ flags 3 rising global risks
item.description:
Neither release is likely to move the New Zealand dollar much on its own. The Financial Stability Report assesses risk rather than signalling policy, and the food price data is only a small input into quarterly inflation. The RBNZ’s warning that recent cost pressures and higher interest rates could reverse the easing in domestic stress points in a cautious direction. Its list of global risks, from Middle East energy disruption to an AI valuation correction, reads like a list of the shocks that tend to hurt risk-sensitive currencies like the kiwi.

---

Coming up later from neighbouring Australia:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock

---

New Zealand food prices fell in October. Meanwhile the RBNZ says the financial system is in good shape, but warns that Middle East conflict, high bond yields and stretched AI valuations could combine into a more severe shock.

Summary:

  • New Zealand food prices fell 0.4% in October from September. The annual rate edged down to 2.3% from 2.4%.
  • Food makes up nearly a fifth of the consumer price index.
  • The RBNZ says global financial stability risks have increased, citing Middle East conflict, higher government bond yields and stretched AI-related valuations.
  • Domestic financial stress has eased from last year’s peak but remains uneven. Smaller businesses and discretionary spending sectors are under the most pressure.
  • Banks hold strong capital and liquidity, and stress tests show the largest banks and insurers could withstand severe shocks.
  • Frontier AI models are speeding up cyber attacks. The RBNZ urged institutions to strengthen their defences and their ability to recover.

New Zealand food prices fell 0.4% in October from September, Statistics New Zealand data showed on Tuesday. The annual rate edged down to 2.3% from 2.4% in September. Separately, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said in its latest Financial Stability Report that the country’s financial system remains resilient, even as global risks have continued to build.

Food prices

Food accounts for nearly a fifth of New Zealand’s consumer price index, so the monthly fall is a modestly softer input ahead of the next quarterly inflation release. The annual rate of 2.3% shows food prices are still rising year on year, only at a slightly slower pace than the month before.

Financial Stability Report

The RBNZ said global financial stability risks have increased, raising the chance of a significant shock reaching New Zealand. Conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt energy and trade flows. Higher government bond yields are adding pressure on heavily indebted countries, and valuations of AI-related firms remain stretched despite recent falls. The central bank warned that growing financial links between AI companies could amplify any further correction. It also warned that these weak points could interact: higher energy costs would feed into inflation and bond yields, and from there into asset prices.

At home, the bank said financial stress has generally eased from last year’s peak but remains uneven. Smaller businesses and sectors that rely on discretionary household spending are under the most pressure. It cautioned that recent cost pressures and higher interest rates could slow or reverse the improvement. The housing market has softened, particularly in Auckland and Wellington, and modest growth in mortgage lending has limited the build-up of housing risk.

Banks hold strong capital and liquidity despite some squeeze on lending margins and profitability. A joint stress test with Australia’s prudential regulator found that the four largest banks could keep lending through a severe downturn. Life and health insurers generally needed several severe shocks before they breached minimum requirements.

The report also flagged frontier AI models as a fast-growing cyber threat, because they speed up attacks and shrink the time available to fix software weaknesses. Governor Anna Breman urged institutions to keep strengthening their cyber defences and their ability to recover quickly from disruptions. 

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Breman 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Army seeks 17 concrete bunkers in Middle East within 45 days as Iran threat persists
item.description:
For oil markets, replacing makeshift shelters with concrete bunkers suggests the US expects its forces to stay exposed to Iranian missile and drone fire for some time. That supports keeping a geopolitical risk premium in crude. This is not a market-moving headline, but it supports the view that the conflict will be long-running, not quickly resolved. Traders may read it as one more reason not to price in an early easing of supply risk across the Gulf.

---

Also:

  • A third US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, has joined two others in the Middle East

---

The Army’s urgent move to swap shipping containers for concrete bunkers in three countries suggests Washington expects its troops in the Middle East to stay under Iranian fire for a long time.

Summary:

  • The US Army plans to build 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers: 10 in Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon.
  • The work must be finished within 45 days of a task order, and contractors are expected to get only three days to submit quotes.
  • The bunkers will replace converted shipping containers now used as personnel shelters, which the Army says leave soldiers at risk.
  • Each bunker is designed to survive indirect fire from missiles and drones, using precast concrete sections, steel doors and sandbag cover.
  • Industry responses are due on 25 November, and exact base locations will only be shared with eligible contractors.
  • Iranian strikes have damaged several US bases in the region, and at least 23 US personnel have died during the conflict.

The US Army is moving to build 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers at bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon, according to an Army notice posted on Friday and reported by Defense News. The work must be finished within 45 days of a task order. The bunkers will replace converted shipping containers that troops are currently using as shelters from missile and drone attacks.

Ten of the bunkers are earmarked for Israel, five for Saudi Arabia and two for Lebanon. The notice names five primary installations: one in Israel, two in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon. Exact base names and locations will only be shared with eligible contractors once a formal solicitation is issued.

The notice is a sources sought request, which is a survey of industry capacity rather than a contract award. Responses are due on 25 November. The Army said the follow-on solicitation is expected to allow only three days for quotes. It cited extreme operational urgency and warned that soldiers are at risk while relying on non-standard container shelters.

The design is built for speed rather than elaborate fortification. Each bunker is made up of three precast concrete sections with steel doors and concrete barriers shielding the entrances. The outer walls are sandbagged, with at least 18 inches of extra sandbag cover on the roof. The bunkers are intended to survive indirect fire, the military term for rockets, missiles and drones launched from beyond the line of sight.

The request follows months of Iranian missile and drone strikes that have damaged several US bases across the region. At least 23 US personnel have died during the conflict, a toll that includes some non-hostile deaths. A March strike on an Army command post in Kuwait killed six service members. The Pentagon sought prefabricated bunkers for the region that same month, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called better protection for troops at Middle East bases a top priority.

Moving from makeshift containers to hardened concrete structures suggests the US expects its forces to remain exposed to Iranian fire for some time, rather than facing a short-lived threat. The next signal to watch is whether the solicitation goes ahead on its accelerated timetable after the 25 November deadline. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock
item.description:
Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock is due to speak from 9.50am Sydney time (2250 GMT, 1750 US Eastern on Monday). She is appearing at the ASIC Annual Forum alongside other regulators. The minutes of the November meeting follow at 11.30am Sydney time (0030 GMT/1930 US Eastern time).

The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, its highest level since November 2008 and the fifth increase of 2026. Six board members voted for the hike and three wanted to hold at 4.60%.

That split is why the minutes matter more than usual. Analysts will look at how the minutes describe the balance of risks between inflation and economic activity, whether the minority thought policy was already restrictive enough, and how high the bar is for further hikes. The RBA’s own assessment puts the current cash rate slightly above the top of its range of neutral rate estimates. It also sees inflation staying above 3% until late 2027.

Markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December hike. Bullock’s remarks will be watched for any sign that persistent inflation and high capacity pressures could justify another increase. Any such signal would push back against that pricing.

Market impact: The Australian dollar has taken the hit from the repricing. It was trading at around 67.6 US cents late on Monday after earlier falling to its lowest level since late January. If either the speech or the minutes leans hawkish, AUD/USD and short-dated yields could get support. If they confirm an extended hold, the currency could fall further. The wage price index is due on Wednesday and October jobs data on Thursday, when unemployment is expected to hold at 4.7%.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Hammack: Economy can handle more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go
item.description:
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack spoke with Bloomberg:

  • Goes into all FOMC meetings with open mind
  • There is not much tension between Fed mandates, inflation going in wrong direction
  • Preference has been for steady, slow rate hike increments
  • ‘I like moving in smaller increments’ to allow economy to adjust to policy changes
  • Inflation pressures appear to be broadening
  • Worried businesses are more accepting of price rises
  • Businesses are passing on more price increases
  • Job market has been largely in balance, but is not dynamic
  • Will continue to express viewpoints
  • With AI, range of impact is very wide
  • Definitely seeing inflation pressures from tech investment
  • Doesn’t see AI investment creating issues for government borrowing costs
  • Higher market borrowing costs needed to restrain economy
  • Financial conditions are still not restraining the economy
  • The economy can deal with more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go
  • 2% inflation is still a reasonable goal for the Fed

Hammack lines up squarely with the Logan-Daly camp and adds the most direct conditions-based argument yet: financial conditions “still not restraining the economy” and higher borrowing costs are “needed” — the mirror image of Bowman’s tightening-has-done-work framing. “The economy can deal with more restriction” is a green light for hikes; “unclear how far the Fed has to go” leaves the terminal rate open-ended, which is the more hawkish read. The broadening story gets anecdotal teeth here — businesses passing on and increasingly comfortable with price rises is exactly the pricing-power dynamic that made the last inflation fight long. Her tactical preference matters though: “smaller increments” and steady pacing takes the Logan-style winter acceleration off her personal table, so she’s hawkish on destination, gradualist on speed. The “not much tension between mandates” line is the kicker — with inflation going the wrong way and jobs balanced, there’s no dual-mandate excuse to stop.

It's still very tough to price in 50 bps this month but the market is increasingly comfortable with three consecutive hikes through March.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tiff Macklem should have been fired, not celebrated
item.description:
Tiff Macklem announced that he will retire after his seven-year term ends in June 2027.

He should have left much sooner.

It continues to baffle me that no central banker paid the price for the disastrous covid inflation. In no other high-profile field in the world is incompetence tolerated to the extent it is in central banking. It's a field that's protected both by government independence and a culture that accepts failure.

No one exemplified that more than Tiff Macklem and his performance during the pandemic.

Despite a raging housing bubble, his bank cut rates to 0.25% in the pandemic. On its own, that's forgivable given the pandemic uncertainty, layoffs and a once-in-a-generation public health event.

Where it went off the rails was with forward guidance that destroyed the central bank's credibility, supercharged the housing bubble, sparked devastating inflation and then led to the subsequent housing crash.

The single individual most responsible for all of that was Tiff Macklem, and yet no one inside or outside the central banking community called for accountability. The worst of his sins was the infamous line that he should forever be remembered by:

“If you've got a mortgage, or you're considering to make a major purchase ... you can be confident that interest rates will be low for a long time," he said on July 15, 2020. “Interest rates are very low and they are going to be there for a long time," he added.

Critically, the assurance was unqualified and unconditional. He was virtually begging Canadians to take on irresponsible debt.

He himself defined "a long time" as "into 2023" in late October 2020 and he reiterated that guidance in January 2021. In that same month he again showed he had no idea what was happening in the economy.

“So far we are not seeing the kind of excessiveness in the housing market that would really get us worried," he said.

Then just three months later -- in April 2021 -- he was signaling rate hikes. In mid-2023 -- the time he said the BOC would first consider hiking -- rates were at 5.00%.

This was the ultimate rug pull for Canadians who took him at his word. In any other field, being that wrong will get you fired. In any self-respecting field it would get you ostracized. In financial markets it would bankrupt you.

There has been no accountability and -- shockingly -- not even any calls for accountability.

Fast-forward to the present. Macklem is dead-set on hiking interest rates once again in a vain effort to salvage his legacy and restore central bank credibility. Today's CPI report was benign but in his personal statue-building, he can't be seen as the man who miserably failed twice on inflation. So like a general fighting the last war, he's over-tightening.

It will be Canadians once again left to pick up the wreckage as he sails into retirement.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Natural gas analysis with the "perfect" trading range
item.description:
Natural gas has a beautiful trading range. Where's the easy entry?

Natural gas futures have repeatedly approached $2.50 and $3.40, creating an almost textbook trading range. But Monday's weakness highlights why an attractive chart pattern does not automatically produce an attractive trade. The $3.20-$3.24 area is now the immediate test.

The daily chart of NYMEX natural gas futures (NG1!) presents something traders love to see: an apparently well-defined trading range, with a floor around $2.50 and a ceiling near $3.40.

It looks almost too good to be true. And that brings us to an important lesson: Knowing where a market might reverse is not the same as knowing when, or whether, to trade that reversal.

The trading range looks remarkably precise

On the continuous futures chart, natural gas reached $2.495 on April 24 and $2.497 on October 26. That's a difference of just $0.002 per MMBtu.

At the upper boundary, the June 1 high of $3.396 was almost identical to the November 11 high of $3.397.

Those matching extremes create an appealing picture of buyers defending the lower boundary and sellers resisting the upper one.

But the latest price action provides an important reality check.

Natural gas reached $3.397 on November 11, retreated, recovered to close at $3.361 on November 12, and then fell to $3.242 on November 13.

On Monday, November 16, the developing daily candle opened at $3.180. Its observed high was just $3.192, below Friday's $3.206 low.

In other words, at the time of this analysis, buyers had not even managed to recover into Friday's trading range.

That shifts our immediate attention away from $3.40.

Natural gas price levels worth watching

$3.20-$3.24: The immediate recovery test

This area combines recent price references with an estimated concentration of trading activity from the previous week.

A recovery into this zone, followed by sustained trading above it, would suggest buyers are regaining some control. Repeated rejection would keep the short-term picture weaker.

$3.09-$3.16: The nearby downside checkpoint

Monday's developing low of $3.089 closely matches the October 28 high of $3.092.

Holding this area could help stabilize prices. Sustained weakness below $3.09 would bring $3.00 and potentially the earlier November base at $2.84-$3.00 into focus.

$3.35-$3.40: The apparent upper boundary

This remains the important overhead region on the continuous daily chart.

Another rejection would support the range interpretation. Sustained trading above $3.40 would challenge it.

These are observation zones, not automatic entry signals or guaranteed targets.

Why a perfect range doesn't offer a perfect trade

Imagine a trader who decides to buy natural gas near the lower boundary of a range.

There are three uncomfortable choices:

  1. Enter early near support. The price may be attractive, with more room toward the opposite boundary. But there is little confirmation that support will hold.

  2. Wait for confirmation. A recovery or successful retest provides better evidence, but often at a less attractive entry price.

  3. Enter somewhere in the middle. The trader may sacrifice both the price advantage of buying near support and the stronger evidence available after confirmation.

There is no free lunch.

The patient trader might watch the market recover without participating. The aggressive trader might get an excellent price, only to discover that the range is breaking.

And even a confirmed reversal can fail.

One additional caution matters here: continuous futures charts combine historical prices from different delivery contracts. Contract changes can create apparent discontinuities, so older boundaries should be checked against the specific futures contract being traded.

What would change the natural gas outlook?

For now, the near-term evidence is weaker than the attractive larger trading range might suggest.

A recovery through $3.20-$3.24 would improve the short-term picture and potentially put $3.35-$3.40 back into consideration.

Continued rejection beneath that recovery zone, especially with prices sustaining below $3.09, would instead increase attention on lower support.

Sideways movement without convincing follow-through remains another possibility.

The educational takeaway is simple: A good trader does not only ask where support and resistance are. The more important question is what price needs to do at those levels to justify taking risk.

Sometimes patience means accepting a worse price for better confirmation. Sometimes it means missing a trade altogether. And sometimes it means avoiding a losing trade.

That is the unavoidable trade-off, even when the chart looks almost perfect.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

What's notable within commodities for traders? Oil traders are caught between a looming long-term supply surplus and immediate geopolitical flashpoints, and right now the chart is sitting on a razor's edge.

While selling activity has recently shown signs of losing momentum with volume shifting higher, a sustained breakdown below $86.75 opens the door to the $77–$79 downside objective, whereas holding above $87.25 would be needed to spark any stabilization toward the daily 20 EMA near $92.

item.title: Fed’s Warsh doesn’t talk about monetary policy in a speech on AI
item.description:
Warsh delivered comments at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco and there's nothing market-moving in them. 

Highlights of the speech:

  • Calls the current era possibly “the most transformational period in my adult lifetime”
  • AI (he calls it SI) “could supercharge idea generation” and sustain growth substantially above the long-run average
  • Productivity growth has been “reasonably strong” in recent quarters but hasn’t yet broken out “definitively and structurally to the upside”
  • The Fed’s role is “neither advocacy nor opposition”
  • Widespread adoption will have “important implications for monetary policy down the road”
  • “We’re certainly not here to make predictions”
  • Board staff has begun modelling scenarios; they’re “illustrative scenarios, not forecasts”
  • Flags risks to critical infrastructure, saying SI “empowers all, including bad actors”
  • “Can you be a superpower without super intelligence?”

If you were looking for a hint on the next move in rates, there’s nothing here. The only mention of monetary policy is that one line about implications “down the road”. There’s nothing on inflation, the neutral rate or the balance sheet.

What you do get is a look at how the Fed is framing the AI question. The staff scenarios are:

  1. Productivity rises, the gains are shared between labor and capital, GDP growth runs persistently above trend and the economy stays near full employment.
  2. Growth still runs above trend but automation displaces jobs and unemployment rises above levels consistent with full employment.
  3. AI disappoints after heavy capital investment and stock market gains. Equity valuations fall, the economy slows and unemployment rises more notably. The economy eventually recovers, “but without the productivity gains.”

I don't think anyone is going take predictions from Warsh on AI and he's not exactly carving out a great reputation for interest rates either, after campaigning for the job on the idea of cutting rates and that inflation was going to fall.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Forget the petro-dollar, introducing the chip-dollar
item.description:
Deutsche Bank’s Mallika Sachdeva is out with a big-picture note arguing that semiconductors have quietly become one of the most important drivers of the US dollar.

The headline stat is a stunner: for the first time in modern history, global trade in semiconductors exceeds trade in oil and gas. That’s based on the four quarters through Q2 2026.

More important for FX is where the surpluses are piling up. Chip surpluses in Asia ex-China (Korea, Taiwan, Japan and ASEAN) have now caught up to the petroleum surpluses in the Gulf.

For 50 years the deal was simple: the Gulf sold oil in dollars and recycled the proceeds into Treasuries. Deutsche argues that regime is being superseded, and rather quickly. The difference this time is where the money goes.

Korea is the case study:

  • Semiconductor exports are up more than 200% y/y this year
  • The chip trade surplus is close to $250 billion
  • Chips account for 100% of Korea’s overall trade surplus
  • Korean purchases of overseas equities have been five times purchases of overseas bonds over the past two years
  • 70% of Korea’s overseas equity holdings are in the US, and it’s 90% for Korean households

So the chip money is going straight back into the US tech companies that are buying the chips. You can see it in the US capital account:

  • Foreign purchases of US equities have topped $1 trillion over the past year
  • That’s more than double foreign buying of Treasuries
  • Even foreign buying of US corporate bonds now exceeds Treasuries
  • Most of the increase in equity buying has come from Asia

Why does the US get to be at the center of this when the chips are made in Asia? Because that’s where the profits go. Deutsche cites research showing 70% of semiconductor industry profits flow to US firms, with US companies controlling 87% of revenue in chip design. The manufacturing happens in countries that are all US-aligned.

There’s also a long runway. Hyperscaler capex commitments are estimated at close to $8 trillion out to 2031, and with chips making up more than half the cost of an AI data center, that implies another $4 trillion in chip demand from AI alone.

The risks are the best part of the note.

The first is circularity. Asian chip surpluses are funding US AI stocks, and those surpluses exist because of demand from US AI companies. If demand for compute doesn’t keep pace with the investment, earnings estimates fall, chip demand falls and the foreign equity bid dries up all at once.

The second is that equities are a far shakier foundation than bonds. Realized volatility in the S&P 500 has been three times that of 10-year Treasuries, the Nasdaq is double the S&P and the Philly Semiconductor Index is more than triple. A dollar that depends on equity inflows should be a more volatile dollar.

China is the outlier. It runs a manufactured goods surplus of more than $2 trillion but a persistent deficit in semiconductors, and it isn’t recycling into US markets. Less than 20% of China’s net international assets are in portfolio investments compared to nearly 50% for Korea, Japan and Taiwan. The preference there is gold and hard assets.

Deutsche’s conclusion is that dollar dominance now rests on US technology leadership rather than geopolitical leadership, and on private balance sheets rather than public ones.

This is a compelling framework and it explains a lot about why the dollar has held up even as the Treasury market lost its foreign sponsorship. When the AI trade finally cracks, the FX market is going to feel it in a way it wouldn’t have in the past. This dynamic is one you can see in the day-to-day moves in the FX and equity market and DB highlights why it won't change any time soon.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says he wouldn’t mind seeing Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
• National security was not put at risk
  • “I don’t know that she was a spy at all"
  • Don’t know that the woman involved with Huang was a Chinese spy
  • Having Huang go back is “not a bad idea”
  • Huang “learned a lesson”
  • On meeting Xi and Putin in China: We’ll talk about denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine; economy and trade too
  • Big meetings on the Asia trip will be mostly on economics
  • May also meet with Kim Jong Un
  • Not considering replacing Lutnick

This whole thing was an incredible hit job coordinated by China hawks.

That’s about as close to an endorsement as it gets without telling the board what to do. It also undercuts the entire premise of the ouster: if the president says there was no security breach and he isn’t convinced she was a spy, what’s left is an affair. He also endorsed Lutnick, who is the guy who didn't put Megaspeed on the entity list.

The comeback campaign is building. The FT has Huang talking with confidants about a return, and Musk is behind a petition that has passed 170,000 signatures. Trump isn’t in step with his own Treasury Secretary though, as Bessent is pushing for a “dramatic shakeup” under an outside CEO. Kress is running the company as interim CEO in the meantime.

The market isn’t buying it yet. NVDA is trading around $162 which is almost flat after falling 4% premarket.

The Nasdaq is off 1.0% after the open, also trimming losses. The five-day loss is close to 13% and the stock sits about 30% below its October high at roughly 17.5x forward earnings. The 52-week low at $148.80 is the level to watch, with earnings due Tuesday.

On the summit, the three leaders sit down Thursday in Shenzhen at APEC. Two of today’s comments go beyond the official script: US officials had said Ukraine wasn’t expected to come up, and no Kim meeting was on the schedule. Expectations are low regardless, since officials aren’t anticipating any concrete agreement and China has resisted three-way arms talks before.

Eyes are on Iran but it's likely safe until after Trump returns home.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs gets bearish on oil prices but doesn't see help for consumers
item.description:
Goldman Sachs is out with its 2027 oil outlook and the title says it all: “Adaptation.”

The theme is that crude prices ran well above pre-war expectations this year, but not nearly as high as you would have guessed if you’d known how long the Hormuz disruptions would last. Mideast supply and global demand both adjusted better than anyone anticipated.

Their forecasts

  • Brent to average $88/bbl in 2027 (spot at $94.11)
  • Easing to $78/bbl by December 2027
  • Fair value falls from $90/bbl today as the market returns to surplus
  • US wholesale diesel to average $150/bbl in 2027

The supply side is where it gets interesting. Goldman’s base case has Mideast supply rising above its 2025 average next year, thanks to ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions, while supply growth elsewhere stalls.

The real story might be in products. Goldman sees crude normalizing but products staying well above average for three reasons:

  1. Slow net refining capacity growth keeps product markets structurally tight
  2. The Mideast conflict continues to support product prices through low exports, high freight rates and deferred maintenance
  3. Russian product output is assumed to remain largely constrained

That’s a world where the headline crude price tells you less and less about what consumers and businesses are paying. Diesel at $150 is a tax on everything that moves, but it's good news for refiners. Note though that the CRAK refiners ETF has come down in the past month.

That ETF and Valero are worth watching and are both down pre-market today.

On risks, Goldman sees them on both sides. The near-term skew is to the upside from intensified shipping attacks, infrastructure damage and a recovery in the risk premium. Note too that a third US aircraft carrier arried in the Middle East this weekend, the first time there has been a trio there since 2003 when the Iraq war began. Further out, Goldman Sachs says the risk is lower prices from stronger supply, weaker demand or a fading risk premium.

The trade recommendation is long summer 2027 European gasoline as a hedge against geopolitical upside. The thinking is that gasoline output could be squeezed by further refinery strikes, heavy planned maintenance and refiners shifting yield toward diesel. They also advise traders to “stay nimble and lean against large swings in risk premia.”

That last line is the best advice in the note. The lesson of 2026 is that the oil market is far more resilient than the worst-case scenarios assumed, and fading the panic has been the right trade more often than not. Then again, I take the bearishness as a sign of complacency on Iran risks.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada October CPI 3.1% vs +3.2% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 3.1%
  • Unrounded 3.09%, unchanged from Prior
  • CPI +0.2% m/m vs +0.3% expected
  • BOC core 2.0% y/y vs 2.2% prior
  • BOC core +0.4% m/m vs +0.0% prior
  • CPI median 2.0% vs 2.0% expected (prior was 1.9%)
  • CPI trim 1.8% vs 1.9% expected (prior was 1.8%)
  • CPI common 2.5% vs 2.4% prior

Details, October vs September (y/y unless noted)

  • Rent +1.7% vs +2.8%
  • Shelter +1.4% vs +1.8%
  • Property taxes +3.8% vs +5.6% (priced once a year, in October)
  • Homeowners’ replacement cost -2.1% vs -1.9%
  • Services +2.1% vs +2.6%
  • Goods +4.3% vs +3.7%
  • Ex food and energy +1.8% vs +2.1%
  • Energy +21.8% vs +19.0%; m/m -1.4% vs +4.2% prior
  • Gasoline m/m -2.5% vs +6.1%
  • Transportation +8.9% vs +8.4%
  • Food +2.4% vs +2.2%
  • Restaurants +3.1% vs +3.1%
  • Clothing and footwear +2.7% vs +1.7%
  • Health and personal care +2.1% vs +1.7%
  • Recreation, education and reading +4.2% vs +4.6%
  • Household operations and furnishings +0.1% vs +0.4%
  • Semi-durable goods +1.2% vs +0.4%

USD/CAD was up 16 pips to 1.4286 ahead of the data and Canadian 10-year notes were trading at a yield of 3.84%. The initial reaction has been to sell the loonie, at that's boosted USD/CAD to 1.4300 while 10s are down to 3.81%.

The Bank of Canada has taken a hawkish stance and this report raises questions on how much that's really needed. Ex-energy CPI rose 2.0% y/y and pump prices are down in November. The BOC is making the case that prices are broadening but there is weakening to, with shelter at just 1.4% y/y and cellular services -6.2%. Trim is running at 1.6% annualized over three months.

A problematic spot in Canada and the US is goods, where prices were up 4.3% y/y. Another thing hawks can point to is clothing, up 3.4% m/m on higher shipping costs. Grocery inflation also ticked up, but at 2.0% it is still below headline for a third month.

Three weeks ago the BoC hiked to 2.5%, the first move in a year, and Macklem said more may be needed. At that point swaps had about a 60% chance of another in December. Governing Council’s own case for holding was that the inflation was concentrated in energy and energy-heavy services like airfares. This report is that argument, with trim moving the wrong way for a hike. December 9 just got a lot harder to justify and the next CPI report isn't until Dec 14.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
